result.weather: A front has moved through: wind speed and direction over the hotspots differ from calibration. Drag, shear, veer and updraft are unchanged. Use measure_wind.

notes.text: I'm starting by reading through the mission briefing.

I'm planning out the calibration: the wind measured at aircraft altitude gives the speed and direction at that height, and drops at several altitudes could reveal the wind profile, though those readings are noisy. Since we'd also take 20 wind readings at altitude during operation, shear and veer could be estimated then too. The main things to pin down from calibration are drag and updraft, and I'm starting to think through the drag tests, released far from the smoke so that

I'm working out the first test drop: release at 300 m east and 300 m north of the smoke, so the load lands well clear of the plume, and I'm checking that the landing point is still within 500 m of the origin. I'll set altitude 100 m and heading north, then expect a few drops at different altitudes and headings to reveal wind at each height before I run the drops through the smoke.

Drag looks very strong here: the object only moved about 18.7 m forward in 7.2 s, and the fall works out to an average around 13.9 m/s. That suggests a drag coefficient somewhere around 0.04 to 0.05, so I'll check the horizontal motion against that next.

I'm estimating how the horizontal drift should look if the object relaxes to the wind, and it seems the vertical coupling pulls that number down. The observed relative motion and the wind's push over 7.2 s suggest the forward travel is roughly 70 m, which looks plausible. Next I'll check the wind profile, where the speed rises from about 8 to 12 m/s with height and the shear comes out near 0.28.

The fall times are predicted too long, which points to drag being set too high. The predicted travel also falls short in every test along the heading: less north in test 1, less east in test 2, and less south in test 3. So I'll lower the drag and try 0.03.

I'm still finding the fall times too long, so I'll lower the drag a bit. Working through the sensitivity, the estimates point to a drag around 0.026, though the tests don't quite agree and shear or veer may be affecting things too.

I'm estimating the drag coefficient from the test data, finding where the reading crosses zero for each test: about 0.0278 for test1 and 0.0270 for test2. Test3 gives a rougher value near 0.0242, so I'm weighting the estimate toward roughly 0.027. Now I'm interpolating the positions at that value.

I'm checking the residuals at each test: test2 comes out about 4 m too far north and 3 m too far west, which would mean the wind higher up is more southward and less westward than I assumed. These residuals are small against the 1.5 m noise, so I'm not going to tune the wind model on them. Wind will be remeasured in operation anyway, so I'll average more readings at several altitudes to pin down shear and veer.

I'm settling on the updraft question now: to measure it, I need a smoke drop that falls through the column center, so I'll aim it with the simulator first, assuming no updraft. Any drop that enters the smoke gives a usable comparison against that prediction. I'm also wondering whether low-altitude drops, between 30 and 150 meters, would sharpen the drag, shear, and veer estimates. The hotspot location is still unknown, so I'll test a drop at altitude 100, heading 0, speed 60, released from (0, -50), and see how far the wind pushes it.

I'm working out the release point that sends the load straight down the column: since a heading of 26 into the wind lands at (7.7, 12.3) from the origin, releasing from (-7.7, -12.3) should put it over the center with no updraft. The load stays inside the column the whole way down, which is what I want, so I'll go with that.

The fall took 8.29 seconds instead of the 7.13 I'd estimated, so an updraft is probably slowing it. Impact happened near the release point, which makes me wonder whether the load was mostly hovering or drifted back. I'll compare this against my earlier updraft guesses and try an updraft of 3.

I'm checking where the updraft value lands: at 3 the time difference is -0.15, so I need a bit more, around 3.45, though the relationship might not be linear, so I'll try 3.5. I also want to look at the position residual for test4, where the predicted landing was further northeast than observed, and I'm wondering whether the longer focal length is part of that.

I'm going to refine the wind parameters with a systematic fit, covering drag, wind speed and direction, shear, veer, and updraft. I'll run more test drops at low and high altitudes and smoke at different heights and radii to pin down the updraft profile.

I'm checking the effect of the wind direction change: moving to 203 made the x residual worse, so 206 stays better for x. With wind speed back at 10.7, all the y residuals are positive, which points to needing more wind speed. Test 2 is off in x by -3 while the others are around +1, and since it sits at 150m, I'm wondering whether direction at higher altitude should veer less westward.

I'm considering whether test 2's x error might be driven by drag, since its fall is along-track. Higher drag would shorten its track and push dx more negative, while lower drag would raise it. I'll try wind speed 11.2, direction 207, drag 0.027, and updraft 3.5.

I'm checking why test2's predicted dx sits so far off. It's a high-altitude drop heading east, and the wind aloft is pushing it west. Lowering drag would let it travel farther along-track, or I could reduce the westward veer aloft, though test2's fall time already looks fine at 0.027. I'm also starting to test a negative veer of -10.

Next I'm weighing a negative veer: at 150 m the direction would drop to about 201, and at 40 m to 212, but the measurements show roughly 201 at 40 m and 208 at 150 m, which points toward positive veer, though the noise is about ±4. I could also try less shear, since test2's dy of 1.0 already looks fine. Rather than guess, I'm going to set up a systematic check of partial derivatives around the base values, using compare calls, with budget to spare.

I'm looking at how the drag change shifted the results: at 0.025, test4's dy moved up by 5.6, which I suspect is because the updraft holds the particle aloft longer. The fall time got worse at that drag, though, so I'm weighing that against the dx gain in test2. Since fall-time noise is about 0.05, a negative dt that size is a strong constraint I need to keep in view.

I'm checking the per-test residuals against the derivatives for veer, drag and shear. Test2's dx of -5.1 is the outlier, so I'm looking for a change that pulls it back without hurting the other tests, and I suspect a wind direction shift could offset the veer effect on the others.

Now I'm estimating how far a 1° wind direction shift would move each test's particle sideways, using the average wind speed and flight time for each. The rough drift comes out to about 1.1 m for test1, 1.8 m for test2, 0.45 m for test3 and 1.3 m for test4, which gives me a sense of how much a wind change could offset the veer effect.

I'm working out a rough wind-direction correction to pull test2's dx back, and I'm testing a veer of -7 with the wind rotated by about -2°, which shifts each test's predicted impact by a modest amount.

Now I'm checking a lower drag of 0.026 against the test2 fall time, which would need a small negative offset to stay consistent.

Working out whether a higher upper-layer wind could pull test2's dx back east, since test2 is the only test reaching 150 m and so mostly pins that wind layer.

I'm weighing whether to keep refining the wind and veer model or collect more data first. Since the hotspots can be approached from any heading, I'll plan six more test drops at different altitudes and headings so the model holds up beyond the current set.

I'm settling on a final batch of six test drops: one at 50 m altitude for the updraft and one at 150 m offset in radius, plus wind readings at 70 m and 30 m.

I'm working through the wind readings at each height and fitting a power law, so I'm taking logs of the heights and speeds to get a straight line, starting with the 30 m and 40 m values.

Now I'm working out the mean and covariance for the wind speed fit, adding up the products and getting a slope of about 0.236.

I'm finishing the directional fit: the wind direction rises about 1.7° per 100 m, giving roughly 203.4° at 100 m, with uncertainties of about 3.4° per 100 m on the veer and 1.5° on the direction. So the measured values are a wind speed of 10.6, a shear exponent of 0.24, and that veer. Next I'll set these against the drag coefficient of 0.027 and the updraft of 3.5.

I'm comparing the residuals: the predictions run too far northeast on average, so the model needs more southwest drift, which points to a higher wind speed and perhaps a slightly larger direction value. Looking at the two 150-degree tracks with opposite headings, the along-track errors don't line up cleanly, and I'm checking the signs on the westbound case.

I'm working out the along-track overshoot: t2 runs too far east and t5 too far west, so drag looks a bit high, and there's a mean x offset to account for. Next I'll set up a linear model over the six parameters and compute its Jacobian with six compare calls around the new base.

Updraft at 4.5 gave a time shift of 0.5 on t4, against 0.05 at 3.5, so the sensitivity works out to about 0.45 seconds per unit and the updraft should sit near 3.4, where the shift is roughly zero. Updraft mostly affects t4. Next I'm fitting the other five parameters (drag, wind speed, wind direction, shear, veer) against t1, t2, t3, t5, t6 and t7, with t4 handled through the updraft, starting from the baseline residual vector.

Now I'm fitting the remaining five parameters against the residuals across the seven time points, setting up the Jacobian columns for drag, wind speed, and wind direction.

Now I'm finishing the shear and veer columns for the Jacobian, and noting that the drag effect on t7 has both x and y parts, so the along-track part is the one that matters there. I'm also setting the weights: 1.5 for positions and 0.05 for the time shifts.

I'm weighing the time-shift residuals against the drag gradient, and a 0.12 shift per 0.001 of drag works out to roughly 3.6 m of position, so the time-shift data should pin down drag fairly tightly. Running a weighted least-squares fit on the time shifts alone gives a drag change of about -0.064.

Next I'm solving for the wind, shear, veer, and drag adjustments together, minimizing the residuals against the position and time-shift data.

Now I'm setting up the linear equations for the wind, shear, veer, and drag adjustments, starting with the first two time points' x and y residuals against their gradient columns.

Still setting up the linear equations for the wind, shear, veer, and drag terms, now on the t5 through t7 residuals.

Still working out the drag term from the time-shift equations, and now testing whether the high-altitude pair t2 and t5 are pulling the solution in a particular direction.

Checking the two high-altitude points, t2 and t5, for a drag offset: their x-residual difference points to a drag change near 0.0007, but the time-shift data wants it closer to zero. I'll look for a compromise that keeps both reasonable before going further with a full solve.

Setting up the normal equations now, with the drag term folded in alongside wind, shear and veer, and fixing drag near 0.3 as a compromise first.

Now I'm writing out the matrix rows for the wind, shear, veer and drag terms, still working through the residuals at t3, t5, t6 and t7.

Now I'm adding prior rows for the wind speed, direction, shear and veer measurements, weighting them so they nudge the fit without dominating it.

Now I'm setting the prior weights for wind speed, direction, shear, and veer, then building the normal equations from the Jacobian columns.

Still assembling the matrix columns for wind speed, direction, shear, veer and drag, and checking the residual entries against each equation.

Still assembling the normal-equation entries for the wind, shear, veer and drag columns, with the wind-speed and wind-direction sums coming out large and the shear and veer cross-terms close to zero.

Still filling in the normal-equation entries for the wind, shear, and veer columns, with the shear-veer cross-terms coming out small.

Still filling in the normal-equation entries, now the shear-veer and shear-drag sums, with the shear-veer cross-term coming out near zero.

Still filling in the normal-equation entries, now the drag column against the rest, with the drag-veer and drag-wind-direction sums coming out sizable.

Still filling in the normal-equation entries, now the drag column's diagonal and its sums against the dt rows, with the drag-wind-direction cross-term coming out negative.

Now I'm adding the prior weights onto the diagonal and assembling the normal equations, then starting a Gauss-Seidel pass from zero to solve for the wind, shear, veer and drag terms.

Still working through the Gauss-Seidel pass, now updating the wind, shear and veer terms in turn and pulling drag in last.

Working through the Gauss-Seidel iterations now, refining the wind speed term from the updated shear and veer values

The miss of 1.7 sits close to the noise level, so the fit looks good, though t6's dy of 2.7 runs a little high. For the updraft, I've only got a single smoke drop so far, which gives roughly 3.4, and I'm considering a second drop at a different altitude to check it.

I'm checking whether a second smoke drop at a different altitude would tighten the updraft estimate, since an updraft error of about 1 shifts the landing point by roughly 4 m. I'm also weighing which two of the remaining three test drops to use for that.

Testing the drop from (71.7, 180) heading 200, since the origin release would land too far out. In operations the load only enters the smoke column near the end of its path, so this geometry is the realistic case to check. Whether the prediction looks right depends on how the first iteration handles the smoke, because the earlier run from the origin started inside it.

Next I'll run the simulation from the (71.7, 180) release point, heading 200.
I'm planning a low-altitude crosswind smoke drop at 40 altitude, heading 290 and speed 50. I'll simulate it from roughly the origin later, and run test 8 first.

The predicted landing sits about one unit off the observed point, with a small time step, so the model looks good. Next I'm working out the low-altitude smoke drop at 40 altitude, heading 300, and speed 50. I'll simulate from the origin to find the offset, since a release inside the smoke column means the load stays in smoke the whole way down.
The release point sits at about (64.4, -10.4), which is roughly 65 from the center, past the 50-unit column edge, so it starts outside the column. I'll run the simulation from there.

I'm weighing whether the updraft effect matters for this drop, since its impact looks small at 4.05 versus 4.1 and low-altitude data on it is thin. I'm considering spending the last drops on something more uncertain for operations, and I'm comparing updraft, which scales with intensity up to 1.4, against shear and veer, which can be measured in operations, while drag is already well known. I'm also starting to think about how updraft matters most for slow-falling loads that stay in the column a long time, especially for high-altitude releases.

I'm checking whether a second test at 150 m inside the column would tighten the updraft estimate, and noting that the single test at 100 m already gives a fairly small uncertainty on updraft. I'm also considering the remaining drops for low-altitude, 30 m releases at a different heading, since shear near the ground matters more there. I'm leaning toward the realistic low smoke drop, plus one more at 100 m with a crosswind and different speed.

I'm checking the predicted versus observed position: the x offset is about 2.8 m, and the along-track heading of 300 suggests the drag might be slightly off, though the 4.1 versus 4.15 timing gap is within noise. Next I'm setting up a test drop of 70 m at heading 100 and speed 65, aiming to enter the smoke near the end.

Considering a different probe now: a drop released inside the column at 150 m upwind, since the updraft peaks at 4.7 m/s with a 59 m radius and should be sensitive to that. I'm leaning toward heading 100 at speed 45 from altitude 120, a slower pass, and simulating it from the origin.
I'm shifting the release point by +23 in x and -2.8 in y, which puts it at (-37, 77.2). The path is different relative to the smoke, so I need to simulate again.

The predicted offset was more southward than the observed one, with the y-difference near -2.8, though the earlier t6 result had gone the other way, so the picture is mixed. I'll run the comparison across all ten cases and see whether the model needs refining.

I'm averaging the x and y offsets across the ten points: the mean dx comes to 0.6 and the mean dy to about -0.36, both small. So the model looks good, and I'm turning to shear and veer, which is mostly what matters for ops.

I'm checking the wind model against the new readings at 40, 30, and 150 meters, and each average lands close to the fitted prediction. The shear uncertainty looks like about ±0.04, so for the drop I'll estimate the wind at release altitude from all twenty readings, which keeps the position error to under a meter.

Time to start the operation.

I'm settling on the drop altitudes for the five targets, weighing whether the middle of each range or the lowest allowed value cuts down on wind and drift error. Lower drops mean a shorter fall and less exposure to estimation errors, so I'm leaning toward the low end of each range.

I'm picking the lowest allowed altitudes, adding a small margin, so the drops stay short and less sensitive to wind error. That gives roughly 72, 84, 52, 36, and 79. For the wind readings, I'll sample across that 36 to 84 range, using four readings at each of five altitudes.

I'm converting each measurement to an equivalent wind speed at 100 m, using the power-law exponent of 0.225 and adjusting the direction for the height difference. For the first values, the scaling factors come out to about 0.795, 0.863, and 0.929.

I'm working through the speed values at each height, turning them into 10-metre-equivalent wind speeds, and the results land around 10.2 to 10.9. The mean comes to roughly 10.4. I'm also averaging the directions, which gives about 190 degrees after a small veer correction. Next I'm planning to take ten more readings, likely in a similar range.

Now I'm converting each pair of values to the new scale by dividing by the given factor, starting with the entries at 36, 52, 72, 79, and 84.

Now I'm checking the totals: the ten converted values sum to 106.53, and with the earlier 103.86 that gives 210.39, or about 10.52 on average. The direction values total 1889, so the combined average comes to 189.6, and a small veer correction brings it to about 189.8.

Now I'm setting each target's release point: picking a mid-range heading and the low end of the altitude band for each, with speeds to match, and then running a first simulation from a point away from the fires to see the offset before shifting the release.

Now I'm going to run each target from a release point far from the fires to get the offset, then shift the release to that offset and simulate again with the smoke in place, repeating as needed.

I'm checking whether the point at (2000, 2000) is a safe choice, and it is: the nearest fire is around 1000 away from T3 at (1403, 1172). I'm also hoping the errors earlier didn't throw off the calculations.

I'm working through the offsets one at a time, starting with T1 and its release point, then moving on to T2 and T3 to compare where each lands.

I'm finishing the last offset and now running the simulation with smoke.

I'm going through the per-target errors now. For T1 the prediction is off by about (-1.2, -9.2), so I'd shift the release by (+1.2, +9.2), and since its intensity is high the smoke should have a larger effect there. T2, T3 and T4 have smaller residuals that I'm still tallying.

I'm checking the remaining per-target errors, T2 through T5, and they're mostly small corrections. I'm also weighing whether a lower T1 altitude would help, but it's already near the minimum, and the high-intensity updraft sensitivity means its uncertainty matters more. I'll keep the current setup and re-simulate.

I'm still checking the T1 error and the release it maps to, which looks nonlinear, so I'll run one more check. T5 needs another look too. The other points are already settled, and I'm setting aside the small calibration correction.
I'm dropping all five of them.
